https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/unidentified.text: Europe Unidentified drone breaches Bulgarian airspace, explodes near pipeline Drone was carrying substantial amount of explosive material, enough to produce explosion that could be heard from considerable distance, says Bulgarian premier Burak Bir and Burc Eruygur 08 August 2026 • Update : 09 August 2026 LONDON / ISTANBUL An unidentified drone on Saturday exploded less than a mile away from a major pipeline near the Romanian border, according to media reports. The drone entered Bulgarian airspace from Romania before exploding 1,000 meters (0,6 miles) from a compressor station of the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, near the former Kardam border checkpoint between the two countries, Bulgarian News Agency BTA reported. No one was injured and there was no damage to buildings, infrastructure or the surrounding agricultural land, according to the report. Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced the incident after an extraordinary meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers. He said the drone had entered from Romanian airspace but had not been detected either in Romania or Bulgaria, adding that there was also no information from NATO's Combined Air Operations Center Torrejon (CAOC TJ) in Spain, which monitors airspace across Southern Europe. "When flying at low altitude, it is not possible to ensure sufficiently dense radar coverage," Radev said during a news conference. He added that the "location of the drone explosion was immediately identified" and confirmed that there were no casualties or damage to buildings or infrastructure. The drone had been carrying a substantial amount of explosive material, enough to produce an explosion that could be heard from a considerable distance, Radev noted. Commenting on the issue, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said that Kyiv is in close contact with the Bulgarian side and are currently establishing all the circumstances and technical facts surrounding the incident. "We are fully open to cooperation with Bulgaria to clarify the details. We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Defense Forces did not deliberately direct any assets toward Bulgaria," Tykhyi told reporters, according to Ukrainian state news agency Ukrinform. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Lando Norris takes F1 Dutch GP pole ahead of Russell and Antonelli Putin says Ukraine, West gain no advantage against Russia Ipswich, Everton and Leeds begin Premier League campaigns with victories Iran claims receiving ‘numerous messages’ from neighbors about new security arrangements despite US threat US tanker aircraft leaves Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base, Defense minister says Injuries reported as roadside bomb targets Syrian security bus near Damascus Egypt, Iran discuss regional de-escalation, implementation of Tehran-Washington memorandum See All Suspect arrested after 2 injured in random stabbings in Netherlands Pope Leo voices concern over 'tragic' situation in Sudan

Courtesy of Anthracite Coal National Park A Wilkes-Barre Record headline on Aug. 15, 1902 File Photo ❮ ❯ 🔊 Listen to this Duryea was the scene of a serious riot at the Warnke Coal Washery during the coal strike of 1902. With coal mines, wash plants, and railroads idle for most of the year, owners of the coal mines wanted to reopen their mines with non-union labor to refurnish stockpiles of coal for the approaching winter. George Warnke, one of the owners of the Warnke Colliery and wash plant, hired nearly 100 coal and iron policemen from Scranton to provide security for the non-union workers in early August 1902. A barbed wire fence was erected around the facility. The result was a riot with shots fired, and Duryea Police Chief Lawrence Cosgrove nearly got shot while he made heroic efforts for a cease-fire on Aug. 15, 1902. “At 2 p.m., a crowd of men collected in front of the washery, and an argument with the coal and iron police was started by someone, and soon some stones were thrown at the police by boys. This started the riot. One of the policemen began shooting, and in a short time, a crowd of a thousand people collected – men, women, and children,” the Wilkes-Barre Record reported on Aug. 15, 1902. The coal and iron police initially used blank cartridges to scare the hostile crowd of striking unionized coal miners. When “showers of stones and other missiles” were thrown, the policemen used real cartridges against the crowd, the Record reported. Cosgrove, who testified days after the riot at a Habeas court proceeding before Luzerne County Court of Sessions Judge Galus L. Halsey, said he heard 12 to 14 shots fired from the coal and iron policemen. John Uravicz, a Lithuanian striker, was the only victim who sustained a gunshot wound to his knee. “Chief of Police Cosgrove ran behind the wire fence and ordered the guards to cease shooting. He says he heard bullets whistle over his head as he ran behind the fence. The guards stopped firing when they saw that he was an officer of the law,” the Record reported. Thomas Joyce, president of Duryea Borough Council, immediately went to the Duryea Burgess office of Dr. John A. Burlington and swore out arrest warrants for the owners of the Warnke Colliery and wash plant, George Warnke, Frederick Warnke, and Jacob Warnke, and several guards, charging them with felonious wounding and inciting a riot. A total of 22 men were arrested, but none were striking coal miners. While Cosgrove was escorting prisoner George Warnke through the crowd, he was pelted by stones, the Record reported. The Record reported George Warnke suffered a head injury, and Harry Collins, a guard, suffered a fractured skull. The Habeas proceeding before Judge Halsey was held at the Luzerne County Courthouse on Public Square, Wilkes-Barre, three days after the riot. After the three-hour habeas proceeding, Judge Halsey dismissed all charges against 19 of the 22 men arrested. The riot at the Warnke Colliery and wash plant in Duryea was considered one of the first in Luzerne County during the 1902 coal strike. Other riots occurred outside collieries in Nanticoke, Wanamie in Newport Township, and Plymouth in late August and during September 1902, resulting in Luzerne County Sheriff Albert H. Jacobs requesting military assistance to keep peace. Local journalism matters, and your support makes it possible. https://www.republicanherald.com/2026/08.text: Dr. Peter Scirmantas accepts a medal from Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys in Vilnius in July. SUBMITTED PHOTO By Ron Devlin | rdevlin@republicanherald.com | Republican Herald PUBLISHED: August 29, 2026 at 12:00 PM EDT | UPDATED: September 1, 2026 at 1:27 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... SHENANDOAH — The memory of his wife’s passing was still fresh when Dr. Peter Skirmantas went to Lithuania in July to accept a medal for her role in establishing the Lithuanian Heritage Museum. Anne Chaikowsky LaVoie Skirmantas died in March, four months before the Lithuanian government formally recognized her efforts. A rush of emotion flowed through Skirmantas as Kestutis Budrys, Lithuania’s foreign minister, presented him with the “Merits of Lithuanians Worldwide Award.” “I was trying not to weep,” confided Skirmantas, 75, a retired history professor. “I wished Anne had lived to get the award.” The award, one of the highest given to people in the Lithuanian diaspora, came three months after Archbishop Lionginas Virbilas visited the heritage museum in Shenandoah, officially designated “Little Lithuania” by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Based in Vilnius, Lithuania’s capital city, Virbilas ministers to Lithuanians worldwide. The archbishop spent a good deal of time in the museum, taking photos and chatting with members of the Knights of Lithuania and the Schuylkill County Lithuanian Women’s Club. Virbilas was not certain, but he thought his grandfather might have worked in Schuylkill County’s coal mines. The Lithuanian government presented its Merit for Lithuanians Worldwide medal to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum in Shenandoah in July. SUBMITTED PHOTO Cultural heritage The Knights of Lithuania Anthracite Council 144 sponsored a Lithuanian museum for many years at Annunciation BVM Catholic Church in Frackville. Several years ago, Anne Skirmantas approached the council with an offer to relocate the museum to the former Chaikowsky Funeral Home in Shenandoah. The funeral home, which was vacant, had been run by her parents, Leonard and Eleanor Chaikowsky. Through the efforts of Peter and Anne Skirmantas, the Knights council and volunteers, including the Chicago-based Sakyns (Roots) Lithuanian group, the archive was moved to the former funeral home at 318 E. Centre St. A repository of 150 years of Lithuanian culture in Schuylkill County, it opened in the fall of 2025. It honored the estimated 100,000 Lithuanians who left their homeland and settled in Pennsylvania’s anthracite region between 1865 and 1915. Lithuanian emigres brought their traditions with them, and built St. George Catholic Church in Shenandoah, the first Lithuanian Catholic church in America. The museum preserved stained glass windows from St. George’s and Our Lady of Siluva, a former Lithuanian parish in Maizeville. A sign bearing Lithuania’s national emblem marks the entrance to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum on Centre Street in Shenandoah. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) A stained‑glass panel from St. George’s Lithuanian Catholic Church in Shenandoah, once the first and largest permanent Lithuanian parish in the United States, is displayed at the Lithuanian Heritage Museum. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) A display highlights the Hill of Crosses in Šiauliai, Lithuania, a 19th‑century site of mourning that grew into a symbol of hope and national identity. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) Show Caption 1 of 3 A sign bearing Lithuania’s national emblem marks the entrance to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum on Centre Street in Shenandoah. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) Expand On display are woven tapestry, wood carvings, religious artifacts and family photos from five or so generations. There’s also a library of books in Lithuanian and English. A unique feature is a scale model of the Hill of Crosses, a shrine of more than 200,000 crosses and crucifixes in Lithuania. Testament to the nation’s faith, 100,000 worshippers turned out when Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass at the shrine in 1993. Anne served as curator of the museum for only eight months before her death, but she left an indelible mark on it. “She breathed new life into the museum,” Peter said. “She was very passionate about it.” Teacher, author, advocate Holder of a degree in theater production from Syracuse University, Anne Skirmantas taught at Los Angeles County High School for the Arts. She served as a stage and production manager for authors and Hollywood personalities, including Shenandoah native Darryl Ponicsan, an author and screenwriter. She wrote two books for Arcadia Press’ Images of America Series. “Shenandoah” was written for the town’s sesquicentennial. “Lithuanians of Schuylkill County” featured an extensive photo archive of the town. The late Anne Chaikowsky LaVoie Skirmantas was curator of the Lithuanian Heritage Museum in Shenandoah. (SUBMITTED PHOTO) In an effort to save it from the wrecking ball, she produced a DVD on St. George’s church. After it was razed in 2010, she co-authored “St. George Church: A Photographic Remembrance.” With Peter, to whom she was married for nine years, she made frequent trips to Lithuania. After receiving the medal, which Minister Budrys referred to as “Anne’s Award,” Peter revisited some of their favorite places in Vilnius. In a park, he saw a jogger wearing a shirt with the slogan “Everything’s going to be all right” on it. Those were the words Anne kept telling him when she was in hospice at St. Luke’s Hospital in Bethlehem. “Was it a coincidence or a message from her?” Peter asked. “I prefer to think of it as a message.” Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Most Popular Most Popular The Golden Kettle brings new dining experience to Pottsville The Golden Kettle brings new dining experience to Pottsville CX-70 blends style, performance to put ‘sport’ in ‘SUV’ CX-70 blends style, performance to put ‘sport’ in ‘SUV’ H.S. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Ebola DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.54 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said. Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported. The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”. Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders. The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported. First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding. The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry. Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces. The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa , which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000. Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one. Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors , including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.
